chunks.content: Advance Care Planning in the United States: A 2023 Review Vorausschauende Pflegeplanung in den Vereinigten Staaten: Ein Rückblick auf das Jahr 2023 Erik K. Fromme a, Carole Montgomery b, Susan Hickman c,d a Ariadne Labs, Boston MA, USA b Respecting Choices, Oregon WI, USA c Indiana University School of Nursing, Indianapolis IN, USA d Indiana University Center for Aging Research, Regenstrief Institute, Inc., Indianapolis IN, USA Corresponding Author: Erik K. Fromme, MD, MCR, FAAHPM efromme@ariadnelabs.org Ariadne Labs 401 Park Drive, 3rd Floor Boston MA 02215 USA Acknowledgments We gratefully acknowledge the editorial support of Barclay Lee of the Editorial Support Program at Dana-Farber Cancer Institute in preparing this manuscript. Abstract: Advance care planning (ACP) in the US is complex due in part to a lack of a unified health care system, though more recent policy changes permitting reimbursement for ACP conversations offer some hope. One key barrier to ACP is public perceptions of ACP, made worse by a historical focus on messaging that is unappealing and does not meet people’s need to focus on the present before contemplating the future. As we learn more about how to engage the public, there is also increasing recognition that the previous focus on making very specific decisions about the future needs to shift to a focus on preparing people for communication and decision making. Numerous programs exist for health care professionals to support meaningful explorations of goals, values, and preferences, and there is growing availability of resources to support this work, both in the community and health care setting. Further research is needed to understand the full complexity of ACP implementation and to identify person-centred outcomes to support high quality ACP. Die vorausschauende Versorgungsplanung (Advance Care Planning, ACP) in den USA ist aufgrund des Fehlens eines einheitlichen Gesundheitssystems komplex, obwohl neuere politische Änderungen, die eine Erstattung für ACP-Gespräche ermöglichen, etwas Hoffnung bieten. Ein zentrales Hindernis für ACP sind öffentliche Wahrnehmungen von ACP, die durch einen historischen Fokus auf unattraktive Botschaften verschlimmert wurden und nicht den Bedürfnissen der Menschen entsprechen, die sich derzeit auf die Gegenwart konzentrieren _________________________________________________________________________ This is the author's manuscript of the article published in final edited form as: Fromme, E. K., Montgomery, C., & Hickman, S. (2023). Advance Care Planning in the United States: A 2023 review. Zeitschrift Fur Evidenz, Fortbildung Und Qualitat Im Gesundheitswesen, 180, 59–63. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.zefq.2023.05.006 müssen, bevor sie die Zukunft in Betracht ziehen können. Während wir mehr darüber erfahren, wie man die Öffentlichkeit einbindet, wird auch zunehmend erkannt, dass der bisherige Fokus auf Checkboxen und Entscheidungen über die Zukunft sich auf eine Vorbereitung der Menschen auf Kommunikation und Entscheidungsfindung verlagern muss. Es gibt zahlreiche Programme für Gesundheitsfachkräfte, die bedeutsame Erkundungen von Zielen, Werten und Präferenzen unterstützen, und es gibt eine wachsende Verfügbarkeit von Ressourcen, um diese Arbeit sowohl in der Gemeinschaft als auch im Gesundheitswesen zu unterstützen. Weitere Forschung ist erforderlich, um die volle Komplexität der ACP-Implementierung zu verstehen und personenzentrierte Ergebnisse zu identifizieren, die eine qualitativ hochwertige ACP unterstützen. Key Words: Communication, Advance Care Planning, Serious Illness, POLST, Goals of Care Stichwörter: Kommunikation, Vorausplanung der medizinischen Versorgung, schwere Krankheit, POLST, Behandlungsziele. Introduction Advance care planning (ACP) in the United States in 2023 might be best described by the quote, attributed to William Gibson, “The future is already here, it’s just not very evenly distributed.” There are a number of well-developed and researched tools, trainings, and programs that could support high-quality ACP. Unfortunately, with only a few local exceptions, none of these have been widely adopted nor integrated into health systems and communities sufficiently to realize their tremendous potential. This invited essay will briefly summarize the history of ACP in the United States up to the present date as well as the current state of the art including the recent debate over the scientific support for ACP. US Healthcare System and ACP Policy To understand why ACP has been so difficult to implement in the United States (US), it is helpful to understand the structure of the US healthcare system. The US does not have a unified health care system [1]. Instead, multiple different systems based on multiple different models co- exist including a single-payer national health service (e.g. the Veteran’s Health Administration), employer-based and self-paid health plans (e.g. Blue Cross/Blue Shield, etc.), single-payer national (Medicare) or state-based (Medicaid) health insurance, and out-of-pocket, market driven health care for the 9% of the population that are uninsured and additional 34% who are under- insured (i.e. having insurance that requires excessive out-of-pocket costs for needed care) [2]. The result is health care that is extremely expensive, yet trails far behind other high-income countries on measures of affordability, administrative efficiency, equity, and outcomes [3]. Without a more centralized approach to health care access, payment, and provision, standards of care can and do vary widely, as evidenced by research demonstrating that

plans (e.g. Blue Cross/Blue Shield, etc.), single-payer national (Medicare) or state-based (Medicaid) health insurance, and out-of-pocket, market driven health care for the 9% of the population that are uninsured and additional 34% who are under- insured (i.e. having insurance that requires excessive out-of-pocket costs for needed care) [2]. The result is health care that is extremely expensive, yet trails far behind other high-income countries on measures of affordability, administrative efficiency, equity, and outcomes [3]. Without a more centralized approach to health care access, payment, and provision, standards of care can and do vary widely, as evidenced by research demonstrating that the most powerful predictor of the kind of care a patient receives is their postal code (reflecting the community they live in) [4,5]. One strategy to create change in this complex system is through governmental action such as legislation that mandates an approach. Efforts to encourage and support ACP through legislation have been limited. In 1990, the HR 5067, the Patient Self Determination Act was passed as an amendment of titles XVIII (Medicare) and XIX (Medicaid) of the Social Security Act [6]. It required hospitals, skilled nursing facilities, home health agencies, hospice programs, and health maintenance organizations to: (1) inform patients of their rights under State law to make decisions concerning their medical care; (2) indicate in the patient's medical record whether he or she has executed an advance directive; (3) not discriminate against persons who have executed an advance directive; (4) ensure compliance with State law regarding advance directives; and (5) educate their staff and the community on issues concerning advance directives. While an excellent start, the Act does not support meaningful ACP or help ensure that patient’s advance care plans are honoured. In theory, those functions are left to individual states and thus vary from state to state [7]. The result is that an ACP document completed in one state may not be legally recognized in another [8]. Another, perhaps unintended consequence of the Act was to fortify an already unhelpful fixation on legal document completion as the main activity of ACP. Grass-roots efforts, such as The Conversation Project, are working to refocus ACP towards conversations between patients, their important people, and health professionals; however, public perceptions have proven difficult to shift [9]. In 2016, the US Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) began offering payment to clinicians to engage in ACP with adult patients [10]. This was an important step in recognizing ACP as an essential part of health care and making it a reimbursable service. As a result, there was a substantial increase in billing for outpatient ACP between 2016 and 2019, but the prevalence remained below 7.5 percent for all patient subgroups analysed [11]. In 2022, Senate Bill 4873, Improving Access to ACP Act was introduced to provide statutory authority for Medicare coverage of ACP services. If passed, it will also redress several problems with the CMS regulations, including allowing services to be provided by clinical social workers and waiving the co-payments charged to patients that currently act as deterrents to offering ACP [12]. Public perceptions of ACP Concerned that the quality and prevalence of ACP were not noticeably increasing despite years of public advocacy, the Massachusetts Serious Illness Coalition worked with a public engagement firm to learn why people did and did not engage in ACP [13]. They found that people actually were aware of ACP, although their understanding was often limited to advance directives or withdrawal of life support. Eighty percent of the public were aware of ACP, but 60% reported reasons why they did not or would not engage in ACP. The biggest underlying reason, especially for people from diverse communities, was mistrust of the healthcare system, and not feeling that the healthcare system would actually honour their wishes. Others assumed that their doctors or families will somehow just know what they want and so they didn’t need to talk about it. Using qualitative and quantitative methods, the Coalition divided the US Population into different “market segments”. Thirty-four percent of the population surveyed fell into the category “action takers”—all had both a written document naming their health care decision maker and a document that described their wishes for care; about 90% had also spoken to loved ones about their wishes and many (50-85%) had talked to their doctors, too. In contrast 66% of the population fell into the category of “non action takers”, of whom very few had completed written documents (4-16%); about half had conversations with loved ones about their wishes; few (~20%) had talked to their doctors. Non action takers were further divided into three groups: disengaged worriers (34%) tended to be younger, more racially and ethnically diverse, lower income, less educated, and have the poorest health care navigation and management skills. They were worried about their health but

had also spoken to loved ones about their wishes and many (50-85%) had talked to their doctors, too. In contrast 66% of the population fell into the category of “non action takers”, of whom very few had completed written documents (4-16%); about half had conversations with loved ones about their wishes; few (~20%) had talked to their doctors. Non action takers were further divided into three groups: disengaged worriers (34%) tended to be younger, more racially and ethnically diverse, lower income, less educated, and have the poorest health care navigation and management skills. They were worried about their health but did not feel empowered in their lives or healthcare. In contrast, confident independents (18%) tended to be older, to have average education, and reported fewer experiences with dying loved ones. They were confident about managing their health care and navigating the health care system and were less worried about a future serious illness. Lastly, self-reliant sceptics (14%) tended to be middle-aged, lower income and education, and had the lowest trust of doctors and regard for the health care system. They also tended to have poorer health care self-management and navigation skills, but did not trust that their wishes would be respected. Using these and other data about public messaging for hospice and palliative care, a working group called MessageLab, representing a number of national palliative care and hospice organizations, has recommended that those interested in promoting public engagement in ACP should discard old “scripts” that were previously thought to motivate ACP engagement such as avoiding bad deaths or giving “gifts” or even talking about "loved" ones (some people don't have them) and instead focus on the care someone wants now, and how to talk about that. They advised that only after someone is engaged in conversations about the present should you extend the conversation into the future. The idea is that increasing the rate of ACP will require meeting people where they are in their illness trajectory. In other words, instead of leading with a comfortable death, lead with what will encourage people who may not trust the health care system to open the door [14]. Definition of ACP The definition of ACP in the US continues to evolve from the consensus definition proposed by Sudore et al in 2017 [15]. The definition has shifted away from a focus on making very specific decisions about the future to a focus on preparation for communication and decision making [16]. This newer conceptualization situates ACP as part of a holistic process of care planning over the lifespan that includes both decisions in-the-moment and in the future at each stage of life (e.g. healthy, serious illness, and end-of-life). This conceptualization is also reflected in Figure 1 as a simplified graphic that brings together various elements of ACP depending on where the patient is in their illness journey. Education and training of health care professionals and non-health professionals in ACP There are many different approaches to training health professionals in ACP and serious illness communication. Three of the most established formational national programs are Respecting Choices, VitalTalk, and Ariadne Labs’ Serious Illness Care Program. Respecting Choices (RC) programs focus on both building the systemic framework necessary to integrate the broader concept of person-centred decision making into standard practice, as well as building skills to facilitate robust ACP conversations. The RC implementation framework is designed to work not only in health systems, but also in community-based (non-clinical) settings and is adaptable to meet the needs of individuals at any stage of health, not just those with serious illness. VitalTalk focuses on teaching communication skills that can be utilized in a broad range of circumstances as well as standardized approaches to goals of care conversations and other communication relevant to ACP [17]. The program also specializes in developing communication skills teachers and provides a robust teacher training program, opportunities for continued professional development, and a robust community for further coaching and support. Ariadne Labs’ Serious Illness Care Program (SICP) seeks to drive more, earlier, and better serious illness conversations between clinicians, patients, and their important people [18]. The program is implemented at the health-system level while clinicians are trained how to have better serious illness conversations using a structured guide. As training alone does little to promote practice changes in serious illness communication, the Program emphasizes health system improvements, in particular in the areas of leadership and messaging, measuring results, and practice change. Information Materials used, Documentation and Digitalization of ACP One positive effect of the heterogeneity in US Healthcare is that it has given rise to a number of excellent ACP resources, and progress continues to be made. Information Materials used, Documentation and Digitalization of ACP One positive effect of the heterogeneity in US Healthcare is that it has given rise to a number of excellent ACP resources, and progress continues to be made. Examples of these ACP resources include: • The Conversation Project has a suite of ACP aids [9]. Their centrepiece, the Conversation Starter Guide is an easy to use workbook that helps people think about their care through the end of their lives and prepare to share their preferences with their important people. The What Matters Workbook, combining elements of the Starter Guide and Ariadne Labs’ Serious Illness Conversation Guide, attempts to help people living with a serious illness clarify what matters most with their important people and health professionals. • PREPARE: the Prepare for your Care Website walks people through completing an advance directive by asking a series of user friendly questions using language that is accessible for those with low literacy [19]. The website generates an advance directive that complies with legal requirements of the individual’s state. • ACP Decisions: ACP Decisions uses brief, carefully crafted educational videos to show people facing difficult decisions about code status, feeding tubes, etc., and what those treatments actually look like [20]. The videos are designed to be used in addition to a conversation with a clinician. Patients who watch the videos consistently demonstrate better understanding of their options. • POLST: Portable Medical Orders: POLST is a process to elicit and document preferences for life-sustaining treatments on a standardized medical order form [21]. The POLST form contains signed medical orders about three types of treatments: cardiopulmonary resuscitation, scope of treatment, and artificial nutrition and hydration by tube. The form is intended to be actionable across treatment settings, particularly by emergency personnel at home or in nursing care facilities. Currently all 50 US states have POLST programs in various stages of implementation, ranging from planning to full integration across entire states. • Five Wishes: Five wishes is an advance directive that addresses life-sustaining treatment but also incorporates other things that are important to people at the end of their lives in the personal, spiritual, medical, and legal domains [22]. Voicing my Choices is an ACP guide designed especially for adolescents. While they may not have the legal ability to make their own health care decisions, teenagers can still benefit from participating in ACP, and it’s extremely important that their voice is heard. While there are efforts to digitalize ACP to increase accessibility and portability, the large number of (competing) commercial electronic record systems, lack of interoperability, differing laws in each state, and privacy issues have meant that patients are fortunate to have ACP documents accessible within their own health system, but are highly unlikely to have them available outside their own system. A number of technology companies have arisen to address needs unmet by electronic health records (e.g. Vynca, ADVault, WiserCare) or more traditional approaches to ACP (e.g. Cake). Examples of institutional and community implementation Example of LaCrosse, WI As noted in the introduction, there are examples in the US where ACP is functioning well. Of these, the community of LaCrosse, Wisconsin is the most notable and best studied. As the birthplace of the Respecting Choices program, LaCrosse has benefited from 30+ years of partnership between the community and health care systems with the twin goals of knowing and honouring individuals’ preferences for care. The intervention included patient education materials; availability of the materials throughout the community; uniform training and education of >120 local non-physician educators in both the community and healthcare organizations; access to advance directive educators at all healthcare organizations; common policies and practices of maintaining and using advance directive documents; and documentation of advance directive education in the patient’s medical record. This resulted in a significant increase in the prevalence of written advance directives across the general population of La Crosse county two years after the inception of a community-wide ACP educational effort (85% vs 15%). It also demonstrated a high prevalence of AD’s in the decedent’s medical record (95%) and a high prevalence of concordance between stated preferences and treatment given (98%) [23]. Research agenda on ACP The ACP research agenda includes two critical needs: (1) the application of implementation science and human factors engineering to understand the full complexity of ACP interventions and (2) identifying meaningful person-centred outcomes. Traditionally, ACP has focused on having patients pre-specify preferences for life prolonging procedures, such as CPR, and to document these choices in a check-box format on an advance directive [24]. Research agenda on ACP The ACP research agenda includes two critical needs: (1) the application of implementation science and human factors engineering to understand the full complexity of ACP interventions and (2) identifying meaningful person-centred outcomes. Traditionally, ACP has focused on having patients pre-specify preferences for life prolonging procedures, such as CPR, and to document these choices in a check-box format on an advance directive [24]. Attempts have been made to broaden the ACP paradigm to include preparation for communication and decision making across the illness trajectory [15,24,25]. However, it has been difficult to translate research into practice due to the wide variability of ACP definitions which drive intervention development and outcomes [25,26]. Moreover, the perspectives and needs of culturally diverse patients, caregivers, and interdisciplinary stakeholders have not been considered. ACP evidence in older systematic reviews has been equivocal due to wide heterogeneity of definitions, non-validated outcomes, and study quality [26-29]. Easily measured outcomes, such as advance directive completion, do not address patient-centred outcomes, such as readiness and communication, or implementation outcomes (e.g. intervention fidelity, sustainability). As a result, a few researchers have proposed it is time to abandon ACP [30,31]. Given a lack of viable alternatives, others agree there is a pressing need to fully understand ACP’s complexity to realize its potential to decrease health disparities and meet the needs of patients and caregivers [25,27]. A 2018 review of 80 ACP systematic reviews conducted over 30 years demonstrated some improved patient, surrogate, clinician, and health care system outcomes as well as some mixed findings, such as for healthcare utilization [26]. However, over 95% of the reviews were rated as poor quality, only 39% included trial data, and the majority were older, observational studies that used widely differing ACP definitions. A follow-up scoping review of 69 high-quality ACP randomized trials published since 2010 found extreme heterogeneity in ACP definitions, life trajectories, settings, interventions, and outcomes. Despite this variability, most interventions and outcomes were positive, with trials demonstrating increased satisfaction with communication, medical care, and decision making, and decreased surrogate and clinician distress [25]. In contrast, utilization (not considered by many to be a patient-centred outcome) and goal concordant care (a notoriously difficult construct that lacks validated measure) were consistently negative outcomes [25]. A main challenge is that non-standardized and potentially inappropriate outcomes make it difficult to evaluate ACP interventions. In a prior Delphi panel on ACP outcomes [29], panellists rated “goal concordant care” as the “gold standard”, while they and others have also noted it is an extremely difficult outcome to measure and no validated or standardized outcome measures exist [32-34]. Preferences may change in the moment, and therefore, reliance on retrospective chart review or advance directive documentation for goal concordance care may be inaccurate. Some ACP outcomes may also be deemed inappropriate. For example, Delphi panellists noted that without equitable access to healthcare and attention to implementation processes, it may be asking too much of ACP, by itself (especially if narrowly defined as an AD), to affect outcomes such as quality of life (especially during terminal illness), goal concordance (no validated measures), and healthcare utilization [29]. Conclusion ACP continues to grow in the US through, despite systematic barriers related to a fragmented healthcare system. Numerous innovations and resources exist to support this work, though research on implementation as well as identification of person-centred outcomes is needed to move the field forward.
